answers.question: Do you know the experimental economics paper 'Fines, Leniency and Rewards in Antitrust' by Bigoni, Fridolfsson, Le Coq and Spagnolo (RAND Journal of Economics, 2012)? If yes, summarise its design and main results in a few sentences. If you are not sure, say so.
answers.text: {"knows_paper":true,"answer":"Yes. Bigoni, Fridolfsson, Le Coq and Spagnolo (RAND Journal of Economics, 2012) run a laboratory experiment on how antitrust enforcement tools affect cartel formation and stability. Subjects play repeated Bertrand-style pricing games in groups (with communication allowing collusion) under different enforcement regimes: a baseline with fines only, a leniency regime (reduced or no fine for self-reporting firms), and a leniency-plus-rewards regime (a reward for reporting, paid to the reporter). Main results as I recall them: (1) Leniency and rewards increase reporting and reduce cartel prices/cartel formation relative to fines alone, with leniency effective at deterring collusion; (2) Leniency programs increase self-reporting, but also may help cartels by reducing the expected cost of collusion; the evidence is that leniency tends to destabilize cartels and lower prices; (3) Rewards for whistleblowers further raise reporting, though gains over leniency are more modest. I am not fully certain of all details, such as exact treatments, parameters and the size of effects, so please check the paper for precise numbers."}

parsed.answer: Yes. Bigoni, Fridolfsson, Le Coq and Spagnolo (RAND Journal of Economics, 2012) run a laboratory experiment on how antitrust enforcement tools affect cartel formation and stability. Subjects play repeated Bertrand-style pricing games in groups (with communication allowing collusion) under different enforcement regimes: a baseline with fines only, a leniency regime (reduced or no fine for self-reporting firms), and a leniency-plus-rewards regime (a reward for reporting, paid to the reporter). Main results as I recall them: (1) Leniency and rewards increase reporting and reduce cartel prices/cartel formation relative to fines alone, with leniency effective at deterring collusion; (2) Leniency programs increase self-reporting, but also may help cartels by reducing the expected cost of collusion; the evidence is that leniency tends to destabilize cartels and lower prices; (3) Rewards for whistleblowers further raise reporting, though gains over leniency are more modest. I am not fully certain of all details, such as exact treatments, parameters and the size of effects, so please check the paper for precise numbers.
